Member 1 · Unit 1 · Data and frame

The data is extremely skewed, and that drives everything

Figure 1.1
  • 57% of establishments have a single worker; a few have thousands.
  • Coefficient of variation = 10.8.
  • Data cleaning: no missing values, no zero workers; totals always add up.
  • Possible recording errors: 7 single-owner businesses report 10,000+ workers (6 exactly 10,001 or 10,002). Kept as official, but flagged.
Skewness makes the mean hard to estimate; the proportion is well-behaved.
Tables 1.1-1.4, Figure 1.1 · output/01_srs
Say: "Figure 1.1 shows the key problem: 57% of establishments have one worker, but a few employ thousands. We cleaned and checked the data and found 7 suspicious values of about 10,000 workers for single-owner businesses. We kept them, as official data, and showed they change the SD from 21.5 to 26.8."

Member 1 · Unit 1 · SRSWOR vs SRSWR

Both CIs contain the truth; the two schemes are practically equal

DesignParameterEstimateSE95% CIExact SE

  • V(SRSWR) / V(SRSWOR) = (N-1)/(N-n) = 1.00026: only 0.026% worse.

Figure 1.3
Tables 1.8-1.11, Figure 1.3 · output/01_srs
Say: "Both confidence intervals contain the true values. The two SEs for the mean differ only because of which establishments each sample happened to include; the exact SE is 0.98 for both. SRSWR is only 0.026% less precise, because n is a tiny fraction of N."

Member 2 · Unit 2 · Gain in precision

Neyman gains 17% for the mean; proportional gains nothing

ParameterRE proportionalRE Neyman
Mean1.0001.167
Proportion1.0270.799

RE = V(SRSWOR) / V(design), exact variances

  • VSRS - Vprop ≈ (1-f)/n · Σ Wh(Ȳh - Ȳ)²: strata explain only 0.02% of S², so no gain.
  • Vprop - VNey = (1/n) · Σ Wh(Sh - S̄)² = 0.137: SDs differ, so Neyman gains.
  • Neyman (optimised for the mean) is worse for P; the allocation optimal for P gives RE 1.04.
Figure 2.1
Tables 2.3-2.7, Figure 2.1 · output/02_stratified
Say: "Figure 2.1 shows why the gain is limited: inside every division most businesses have one or two workers and a few have thousands. Cochran's formulas explain the results exactly: proportional gains come from different means, and here they barely differ; Neyman's extra gain comes from different SDs, 17% here. Neyman was optimised for the mean, so it is worse for the proportion."
Member 2 · Unit 2 · ANOVA and basis of stratification

ANOVA: H0 all stratum means equal (5% level)

Test (proportional sample, n = 748)Statisticp-value
One-way ANOVA, F(3, 744)0.3770.770
Kruskal-Wallis (no normality needed)18.280.0004
  • ANOVA: do not reject H0. Normality fails (skewness 267), and a few huge values hide the differences.
  • Kruskal-Wallis on ranks: reject H0.
  • Extra: activity type is the better basis for P (RE 1.13; female ownership 4.7% to 42.1%).
Figure 2.3
Tables 2.8-2.11, Figure 2.3 · output/02_stratified
Say: "The ANOVA on my sample gives F = 0.377, p = 0.770, so I do not reject H0: ANOVA assumes normal data, and a few huge values inflate the within-group variance. The Kruskal-Wallis test, which uses ranks, gives p = 0.0004, so I reject H0. As an extra, activity type would be a better basis for the proportion."
Member 3 · Unit 3 · Systematic sample

k = 3,851, random start r = 975, and all 3,851 possible samples

  • List ordered by location code; every 3,851th establishment from r = 975.
  • Our sample: mean 2.397 (SE 0.248), P 0.1912 (SE 0.0144).
  • Average of all 3,851 sample means = true value exactly, so the estimator is unbiased.
  • CIs containing the truth: 61% for the mean, 96% for P.
The mean's CIs fail because most samples miss the rare giant establishments.
Figure 3.1
Tables 3.1-3.3, Figure 3.1 · output/03_systematic
Say: "With N = 2,880,548 and n = 748 the interval is exactly 3,851; our random start was 975. There are only 3,851 possible samples, so I calculated all of them. Figure 3.1 shows they average exactly to the true value, so the estimator is unbiased."
Member 3 · Unit 3 · Comparison and ANOVA

Best design for the proportion: 12% better than SRS

Figure 3.2: no trend or periodicity

Say: "Systematic sampling is 12% more efficient than SRS for the proportion, better than stratifying by division, because walking down a location-ordered list spreads the sample over every district and town. The ANOVA confirms the starting point doesn't matter, and Figure 3.2 shows no trend or periodic pattern."

Member 5 · F-tests and 500-repeat simulation

F-tests work for P; for the mean, normality fails

500 repeats, F(499, 499), proportionF (p)Agrees with exact?
SRSWOR vs Stratified (Neyman)1.28 (0.0027)yes
SRSWOR vs Systematic1.21 (0.017)yes
SRSWOR vs Cluster22.1 (< 0.0001)yes
  • H0: equal variances · H1: the larger is less precise · 5% level.
  • P: simulated SE within 5% of exact; CIs cover 94 to 97% (cluster 80%).
  • Mean: estimates very skewed, CIs cover only 60 to 64%; one F-test even points the wrong way.
Figure 5.4: 500 estimates of P per design
Tables 5.2-5.4, Figures 5.3-5.4 · output/05_comparison
Say: "We repeated every design 500 times. For the proportion the variance formulas are confirmed and every F-test agrees with the exact variances. For the mean the estimates are so skewed that the F-test's normality assumption fails; one F-test even points the wrong way. That shows why the assumption matters."
Member 5 · Recommendation and official statistics

Recommendation: systematic sampling on the location-ordered list

  • Precision: best for P (RE 1.12), as good as SRS for the mean (RE 1.01).
  • Cost: one random number, then every 3,851th establishment.
  • Convenience: automatically spread over every district.
  • If the mean matters most: Neyman stratified. Cluster: cheapest, least precise (RE 0.04 for P).
Official statistics link: Sixth Economic Census
AgencyCSO, MoSPI, with State DES
DesignComplete count, no sampling
CollectionFace-to-face, every structure in 2.45 million census EBs, Jan 2013-Apr 2014
PurposeA frame for follow-up sample surveys (NSS)
LimitsExcludes crop production, plantation and public administration; misses informal units
Table 5.5 · official facts from the MoSPI EC6 documentation on the census DVD
Say: "We recommend systematic sampling from the location-ordered census list: precise for the proportion, as good as SRS for the mean, and simple and cheap. Our data comes from the Economic Census by MoSPI's CSO, a complete count used as the frame for official sample surveys, which is exactly how we used it."
Conclusion

What we learned

  • A design helps only if it uses structure in the data: stratification needs different groups, systematic needs a meaningful order, and clustering suffers when groups are internally alike.
  • With extremely skewed data (median 1, max 14,160) no design estimates the mean much better than SRS; the proportion is easy.
  • Single-sample SEs and F-tests can mislead with skewed data; exact variances and simulation reveal the truth.
  • Recommended: systematic sampling on the location-ordered census list.
Thank you
